title: Forgiveness, Healing and Unlikely Company
overview: Jesus forgives, heals and eats with people others avoided, drawing both amazed crowds and sharp criticism from religious leaders.

parts.label: Forgiving a paralyzed man (vv. 1-8)
parts.note: The teachers of the law believed only God could forgive sins, so they heard Jesus' words as blasphemy, meaning an insult to God. Anyone can say "you are forgiven" without proof, so Jesus heals the man as visible evidence that he, the "Son of Man" (his usual way of referring to himself), has that authority.

parts.label: Dinner with tax collectors (vv. 9-13)
parts.note: Tax collectors gathered money for rulers backed by Rome and were widely seen as cheats and collaborators, so sharing a meal with them signaled acceptance. When the Pharisees, a movement devoted to careful keeping of God's law, objected, Jesus compared himself to a doctor and quoted the prophet Hosea, where God values mercy over religious ritual.

parts.label: Why no fasting (vv. 14-17)
parts.note: Going without food was a sign of devotion and longing, but Jesus says wedding guests do not fast while the groom is with them; Christians read the groom being "taken" as a hint of his death. Fresh wine still expanding would split old, brittle skins, which suggests that what Jesus brings will not fit neatly into old patterns.

parts.label: A dead girl, a bleeding woman (vv. 18-26)
parts.note: Under the law, the woman's twelve years of bleeding made her ritually unclean, keeping her on the edges of community life, yet Jesus calls her "daughter" and credits her faith. At the leader's house, flute players and a noisy crowd of mourners, a normal part of funerals then, have already gathered, and Jesus raises the girl who has died.

parts.label: Blind men and a silent man (vv. 27-34)
parts.note: "Son of David" was a title for the promised king from David's family line, so the blind men are hinting at who they think Jesus is. Scholars debate why he tells them to stay quiet, and when he frees a man who could not speak, the Pharisees claim his power comes from the ruler of demons.

parts.label: Sheep without a shepherd (vv. 35-38)
parts.note: The image echoes older complaints in Israel's scriptures about people left without good leaders. The "harvest" pictures many people ready to respond, and this call for more workers leads into the next chapter, where Jesus sends out his twelve closest followers.

think: Jesus is criticized here for who he chooses to eat with; who would people be surprised to see at your table, and what makes those lines feel important?
